# PBCPB Phase 0 — Commission Brief 2. external data sources: we will not use external data sources for this playbook ## Purpose Statement
Build a playbook for developing and commercially releasing creative VST audio plugins using the JUCE framework in C++. The playbook guides a single developer — assisted by Claude Code — through the full product lifecycle: from sound design research and DSP implementation through UI design, DAW testing, licensing integration, marketplace listing, and sales strategy.
### Problem Being Solved
The VST plugin marketplace in 2026 is saturated with uninspired, overpriced products that lack creative ambition. Most plugins copy existing designs rather than exploring novel sonic territory. Meanwhile, the tools to build creative alternatives (JUCE, C++, AI coding assistants) have become accessible to solo developers. This playbook enables an enthusiast developer to create genuinely creative, high-quality plugins and bring them to market at consumer-friendly price points — competing on imagination rather than budget.
- minimal role complexity - complex bridged knowledge - standard process complexity - new playbook to test the playbook creator playbook system on it's own ### Target User
A single developer using ai and ai agents to develop the product and entire business with:
- **Strong:** Python/JavaScript, general programming concepts, VST usage as a musician - **Basic:** C++ theory (knows concepts, not fluent), sound design fundamentals - **None:** JUCE framework, DSP algorithm implementation, commercial plugin distribution - **AI tooling:** Claude Code ($200/month plan maximum), willing to use multiple sessions per feature, multiple limit-hits expected per build cycle - **Platform:** Linux Mint, REAPER for DAW testing
### What This Playbook Must Produce
A developer following this playbook with Claude Code assistance can: 1. Build a functional VST3 plugin (synthesizer, effect, module, or tool) using JUCE and C++ 2. Implement DSP algorithms informed by sound design research (psychedelic, ambient, creative, psybient techniques) 3. Design a clean, modern UI following audio plugin interface standards 4. Integrate a commercial licensing system to protect against piracy 5. List and sell the plugin on KVR Audio, Plugin Boutique, or equivalent marketplaces 6. Execute a marketing strategy achievable by a solo developer with minimal capital
## Scope
### In Scope
**Development:** - VST3 audio plugin development using JUCE 8.0.x framework and C++17 - CMake build system with FetchContent for dependency management - DSP algorithm research and implementation for synthesizers, effects, modules, and tools - Audio thread safety, gain staging, parameter management, state serialization - Modern audio plugin UI/UX design — synthesizer control layout theory, knob/slider/meter design - Preset system design and sound design methodology - Unit testing with Catch2, DAW testing in REAPER
**Sound Design Knowledge Base:** - General synthesizer sound design theory (subtractive, FM, wavetable, granular, additive, hybrid) - Synthesizer patch creation theory and methodology - Synth module sound design (oscillators, filters, modulation routing) - Core focus areas (use as seeds for expanded research): psychedelic, ambient, pad, creative, psybient sound design - Abstract and experimental sound design techniques - Sources: academic papers, professional textbooks (Pirkle, Zölzer, Smith), expert tutorials, standard references
**Commercial:** - VST plugin marketing strategies for 2026 marketplace conditions - Commercial licensing systems (PACE iLok, eLicenser, custom solutions, open-source alternatives) - Anti-piracy countermeasures effective for KVR Audio and similar marketplaces - Marketplace listing strategies: KVR Audio, Plugin Boutique, direct sales - Pricing strategy for indie developers targeting average consumer budgets - Full business plan for a solo developer VST product launch
**Reference Material:** - C++ documentation curated for audio relevance (not a general C++ textbook) - JUCE framework documentation and patterns - DSP algorithm references - UI/UX design references for audio software
### Out of Scope - Cross-platform builds beyond Linux (future version consideration) - Hardware integration or physical product design - DAWs other than REAPER for testing (v1.0) - Multi-developer team workflows - Mobile/embedded audio development
### Adjacent - Claude Code skill development for JUCE-specific assistance - Knowledge base maintenance beyond initial bootstrapping - Post-launch analytics and A/B testing
## Constraints
### Budget - Claude AI: $200/month maximum (currently $100, may upgrade) - External tooling: prefer freely available libraries and tools unless planning phase identifies a paid tool as essential — in which case, document cost and justification - No significant capital investment assumed — all recommendations must be viable for a solo enthusiast developer
### Technical Stack
| Component | Version | |-----------|---------| | C++ | C++17 | | CMake | 3.22+ | | Compiler | GCC 7+ or Clang 6+ | | JUCE | 8.0.x | | VST3 SDK | 3.8.x | | AAX SDK | Latest compatible | | Platform | Linux Mint | | DAW | REAPER | | Build method | FetchContent |
### Required Linux Dependencies
``` libx11-xcb-dev libxcb-util-dev libxcb-cursor-dev libxcb-xkb-dev libxkbcommon-dev libxkbcommon-x11-dev libfontconfig1-dev libcairo2-dev libgtkmm-3.0-dev libsqlite3-dev libxcb-keysyms1-dev ```
### Process Constraints - Single developer + AI assistant workflow (role-based-single-agent) - Multiple Claude Code sessions expected per major feature — playbook must define session boundaries that respect token budget - Human makes all creative decisions (sound identity, aesthetic direction, signal flow, target genre) - AI handles DSP implementation, code generation, research synthesis — human reviews and directs - C++ KB content must be curated for audio relevance, not exhaustive
## Success Criteria
1. **Product:** A working VST3 plugin that loads in REAPER, processes or generates audio correctly, has a functional modern UI, and saves/loads presets 2. **Quality:** Plugin passes audio thread safety audit, gain staging verification, and unit tests 3. **Commercial readiness:** Licensing system integrated, marketplace listing prepared, pricing strategy documented 4. **Business plan:** Complete marketing strategy covering pre-launch, launch, and post-launch activities achievable by a solo developer 5. **Knowledge base:** Structured multi-layer KB (Technical, Sound Design, UI/UX, Commercial, Reference) populated with enough content that Claude Code produces informed implementations at every phase 6. **Reproducible:** Another developer with similar skills could follow this playbook and produce a comparable result

## Purpose Statement

Build a playbook for developing and commercially releasing creative VST audio plugins using the JUCE framework in C++. The playbook guides a single developer — assisted by Claude Code — through the full product lifecycle: from sound design research and DSP implementation through UI design, DAW testing, licensing integration, marketplace listing, and sales strategy.

## Problem Being Solved

The VST plugin marketplace in 2026 is saturated with uninspired, overpriced products that lack creative ambition. Most plugins copy existing designs rather than exploring novel sonic territory. Meanwhile, the tools to build creative alternatives (JUCE, C++, AI coding assistants) have become accessible to solo developers. This playbook enables an enthusiast developer to create genuinely creative, high-quality plugins and bring them to market at consumer-friendly price points — competing on imagination rather than budget.

## Target User

A single developer using AI and AI agents to develop the product and entire business with:

- **Strong:** Python/JavaScript, general programming concepts, VST usage as a musician
- **Basic:** C++ theory (knows concepts, not fluent), sound design fundamentals
- **None:** JUCE framework, DSP algorithm implementation, commercial plugin distribution
- **AI tooling:** Claude Code ($200/month plan maximum), willing to use multiple sessions per feature, multiple limit-hits expected per build cycle
- **Platform:** Linux Mint, REAPER for DAW testing

## Project Overview

This playbook covers:
- VST3 audio plugin development using JUCE 8.0.x and C++17
- DSP algorithm research and implementation for synthesizers, effects, modules, and tools
- Modern audio plugin UI/UX design
- Commercial licensing integration
- Marketplace listing and sales strategy
- Marketing execution for solo developers

## Delivers

A developer following this playbook with Claude Code assistance can:
1. Build a functional VST3 plugin using JUCE and C++
2. Implement DSP algorithms informed by sound design research
3. Design a clean, modern UI following audio plugin standards
4. Integrate a commercial licensing system
5. List and sell the plugin on marketplaces
6. Execute a marketing strategy achievable by a solo developer

## Knowledge Base Architecture

Structured five-layer knowledge base with bridge mechanisms:

1. **Technical** — C++17, JUCE, CMake, DSP, VST3/AAX, audio thread safety
2. **Sound Design** — Synthesis theory, patch methodology, creative techniques
3. **UI/UX** — Audio plugin interface standards, control layout theory
4. **Commercial** — Marketplaces, licensing, anti-piracy, pricing, marketing
5. **Reference** — Academic sources, textbooks, expert material

Bridge layer between Sound Design and Technical KBs for descriptor-to-parameter translation.

## Related Playbooks

**None integrated.** This playbook is standalone and self-contained. Existing VST development playbooks in the system are NOT used as input or reference — this tests the playbook-creator-playbook system independently.

## PACE Anti-Piracy & iLok Platform
**PACE Anti-Piracy** is the industry leader in pro audio plugin licensing, with over 40 years of experience and 600+ publishers using their platform. Key offerings include:
### Activation Options: - **iLok USB Dongle** - Physical hardware for offline license storage - **iLok Cloud** - Virtual cloud-based licensing (requires constant internet) - **Machine Activation** - License tied to specific computer
### Protection Levels: - **Level 1 (Wrapper)** - Basic binary protection without code changes - **Level 2 (Fusion)** - Advanced binary hardening with code obfuscation and white-box cryptography - **Content Protection** - For digital content without executable components
## Alternatives to PACE/iLok
### 1. **MuseHub DRM** - **No-code DRM** - Quick implementation without coding - **SDK Integration** - More control for advanced users - Built into MuseHub's distribution platform - Cost-effective for smaller developers
### 2. **Cryptlex** - Modern cloud-based licensing platform - Designed for easy integration - Detailed analytics on license usage - Growing traction but newer than PACE
### 3. **Proprietary Solutions** (Waves Central, Native Access, Arturia Software Center) - Company-specific license managers - Can offer smoother UX tailored to specific products - Requires developing and maintaining your own system
### 4. **Older Methods** - **Serial Numbers** - Simple but easily pirated - **Challenge/Response** - More secure than serials but can be clunky
## Key Considerations for 2025-2026
The search results indicate the industry is trending toward: - **Cloud-based licensing** becoming more prevalent - **Hybrid solutions** offering both online and offline options - **Subscription models** alongside perpetual licenses - **Integration with e-commerce platforms** (e.g., PACE's Shopify integration)

## VST3 Plugin Development Best Practices (JUCE Framework)
Based on my search, here are the key best practices for VST3 plugin development using the JUCE framework:
---
### 1. **Controller ↔ Processor Communication (Critical)**
The most important architectural consideration in VST3 is proper communication between the Controller (UI) and Processor (audio engine):
**Key Rules:** - **Never assume shared memory** - Controller and Processor can be in different threads or processes - **Treat `notify()` as real-time sensitive** - Do minimal work, no allocations, no blocking - **Use bounded queues** - Fixed-capacity buffers prevent unbounded memory growth - **Avoid per-event `notify()` calls for bulk data** - Batch and snapshot instead
**Recommended Pattern for Small/Infrequent Messages:** ```cpp // Use lock-free concurrent queues (e.g., moodycamel::ConcurrentQueue) moodycamel::ConcurrentQueue<MidiPacked_t> m_queue;
// In notify() - RT-sensitive context tresult PLUGIN_API Controller::notify(IMessage* message) { // Minimal work: copy and enqueue only MidiPacked_t e; std::memcpy(&e, ptr, sizeof(e)); m_queue.enqueue(e); return kResultOk; } ```
**For Bulk Messages:** Use double-buffered snapshots with atomic handoffs to avoid data races and allocations.
---
### 2. **Memory Management & Real-Time Safety**
- **No dynamic allocation on audio thread** - Pre-allocate all buffers - **Use fixed-capacity containers** - Know your worst-case memory usage - **Avoid `std::vector::push_back()` in RT contexts** - Unbounded growth is dangerous - **High-water marks** - Set thresholds for graceful degradation instead of crashes
---
### 3. **Data Layout & Serialization**
- **Don't use `#pragma pack(1)`** - Can cause misaligned access and ABI issues - **Serialize explicitly** - Don't rely on struct layout across boundaries - **Use explicit byte buffers** for message payloads
---
### 4. **Plugin Packaging & Distribution (JUCE-Specific)**
**Installation Locations:**
| Platform | Format | Path | |----------|--------|------| | **macOS** | VST3 (User) | `~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3` | | **macOS** | VST3 (System) | `/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3` | | **Windows** | VST3 | `C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST3` |
**Best Practices:** - Create proper installers (Inno Setup for Windows, Packages/dmg for macOS) - Code-sign AUv3 and AAX plugins (required) - Use dynamic runtime linking on Windows (static linking deprecated, limited to 64 plugins loaded) - Provide clear descriptions for all permissions (microphone, camera access) - Test on real DAWs before release - snapshot tests alone aren't enough
---
### 5. **SDK Design Principles**
From the SDK development article: - **Keep the surface small** - Every export is a permanent contract - **Sensible defaults** - Most secure/correct behavior out of the box - **Typed error classes** - Make errors actionable and prefixed with SDK name - **TypeScript/typed interfaces** - Types ARE documentation - **Document-as-code** - Use JSDoc/Tutorials where developers read (IDE tooltips) - **Semantic versioning** - Communicate breaking changes clearly
---
### 6. **Debugging Setup**
JUCE provides a built-in plugin host at `extras/AudioPluginHost/` for testing: - Scan for VST3 plugins in your build output - Configure IDE to launch Plugin Host for step-through debugging - Set breakpoints directly in your plugin code while hosted
---
### 7. **Common Pitfalls to Avoid**
- Don't rely on "it works on my DAW" - Hosts vary in timing, threading, and batching - Don't block the audio thread for *any* reason - Don't assume message ordering or timing semantics - Don't skip marketplace submission requirements (icons, permissions, descriptions) - Don't put environment-specific logic or secrets in SDK core
---
### Resources Referenced
1. **VST3 Controller-Processor Communication** - Detailed technical article on bounded messaging patterns 2. **JUCE Tutorial: Create Basic Audio/MIDI Plugin** - Setup guide with debugging configuration 3. **JUCE Tutorial: Package Your Plugin** - Distribution and marketplace submission 4. **JUCE Forum** - Community discussions on release builds

I found several excellent resources covering synthesizer sound design theory across subtractive, FM, wavetable, and granular synthesis. Here's a comprehensive summary of the key information:
## **Core Synthesis Types Explained**
### **1. Subtractive Synthesis** **How it works:** Start with harmonically rich waveforms (saw, square, triangle) and sculpt away frequencies using filters.
**Key components:** - **Oscillators** - Generate basic waveforms (sine, sawtooth, square, triangle) - **Filters** - Low-pass, high-pass, band-pass to remove frequencies - **Envelopes (ADSR)** - Shape amplitude over time (Attack, Decay, Sustain, Release) - **LFOs** - Create modulation effects
**Famous examples:** Moog Minimoog, Roland Juno-106, Arturia Mini V
**Best for:** Classic analog-style leads, pads, and basses with warm, familiar tones
---
### **2. FM (Frequency Modulation) Synthesis** **How it works:** One waveform (modulator) changes the frequency of another waveform (carrier) at audio rates, creating complex harmonics.
**Key concepts:** - Uses **operators** (oscillator + envelope combinations) - **Carrier-to-modulator ratios** determine harmonic relationships - **Modulation index** controls complexity and harmonics
**Famous examples:** Yamaha DX7, Native Instruments FM8, Ableton Operator
**Best for:** Bell-like tones, metallic sounds, aggressive basslines, inharmonic timbres
---
### **3. Wavetable Synthesis** **How it works:** Uses sample-based waveforms stored in tables that can be morphed between in real-time.
**Key features:** - **Wavetable position** - Sweeps through different waveforms - **Morphing** - Creates evolving, dynamic textures - **Custom wavetables** - Import samples or draw your own
**Famous examples:** Xfer Serum, Waldorf Blofeld, Ableton Wavetable, Vital
**Best for:** Modern bass design, evolving pads, aggressive electronic textures
---
### **4. Granular Synthesis** **How it works:** Breaks audio into tiny fragments called "grains" (1-200ms) that are rearranged and manipulated.
**Key parameters:** - **Grain size** - Duration of each grain - **Density** - Number of grains playing simultaneously - **Position** - Where in the sample grains are read from - **Randomization** - Adds organic variation to pitch, position, timing
**Famous examples:** Ableton Granulator II, Arturia Pigments granular engine, Robert Henke's Max4Live Granulator II
**Best for:** Atmospheric pads, experimental textures, time-stretching independent of pitch
---
## **Additional Synthesis Types Worth Knowing**
### **Additive Synthesis** Builds sounds by combining sine waves (partials) at different frequencies and amplitudes. Great for bells and inharmonic timbres.
### **Physical Modeling** Uses mathematical algorithms to simulate real-world instruments (strings, drums, wind instruments). Examples: Arturia Pianoteq, Ableton Tension.
### **Phase Distortion** Manipulates the phase of a waveform to create new harmonics. Digital alternative to FM with sharp, complex tones.
### **Spectral Synthesis** Analyzes and manipulates the frequency spectrum directly. Allows precise control over individual harmonics.
### **Vector Synthesis** Blends multiple sound sources in a 2D space for real-time morphing between up to four sources.
---
## **Advanced Sound Design Techniques**
1. **Layering multiple synthesis types** - Combine additive pads with subtractive basslines 2. **Modulation matrix routing** - Assign LFOs to multiple parameters simultaneously 3. **Macro controls** - Single knob controlling multiple parameters for performance 4. **Microtonal scales** - Use intervals smaller than semitones for unique harmonies
---
## **Key Takeaways**
- **Subtractive** is beginner-friendly and great for classic tones - **FM** excels at complex, inharmonic sounds but has a steeper learning curve - **Wavetable** offers modern, evolving textures with extensive customization - **Granular** transforms any audio into lush, atmospheric textures
Each synthesis method has unique strengths, and modern synthesizers often combine multiple types for maximum creative flexibility. The best approach is to start with subtractive synthesis fundamentals, then explore FM and wavetable synthesis, and finally experiment with granular synthesis for more experimental sound design.

I found several excellent resources on audio DSP implementation and real-time safety best practices. Here's a comprehensive summary of the key findings:
## Key Results Summary
### 1. **LLVM's Real-Time Safety Revolution (ADC 2024)**
**RealtimeSanitizer (RTSan)** is now coming to mainline Clang, providing two major tools:
- **Runtime Detection**: Detects calls to `malloc`, system calls, and other "unsafe" functions during execution of non-blocking functions - **Compile-Time Performance Constraints**: New Clang feature that prevents blocking function calls from non-blocking functions at compile time
Example error messages you'll see: ``` "Error: RealtimeSanitizer: call to malloc detected during execution of nonblocking function MyAudioCallback::process!" "Warning (-Wfunction-effects): nonblocking function `MyAudioCallback::process` must not call blocking function `SketchyCall`" ```
---
### 2. **Memory Ordering Best Practices (Bruce Dawson, Feb 2025)**
**Key recommendations:**
- **Avoid `std::mutex`** in real-time audio threads because: - Non-deterministic latency from thread contention - Priority inversion issues - Can block the audio thread
- **Use `std::atomic` with proper memory ordering:** - Prefer `std::memory_order_release` and `std::memory_order_acquire` over default `std::memory_order_seq_cst` - The default sequential consistency imposes unnecessary performance costs
Example pattern: ```cpp std::atomic<float> gain{1.f};
// Control thread (UI) void updateGain(float newGain) { gain.store(newGain, std::memory_order_release); }
// Audio thread float processAudio() { return gain.load(std::memory_order_acquire); } ```
---
### 3. **Spinlocks for Real-Time Audio (timur.audio)**
**Critical findings:**
- **Never use `std::mutex::try_lock()`** on the audio thread! The `unlock()` can trigger system calls when other threads are waiting - **Spinlocks are better but have trade-offs:** - Basic spinlocks burn CPU cycles at ~200 million iterations/second - Can starve other threads on the same core
**Recommended `audio_spin_mutex` implementation** with exponential back-off:
```cpp struct audio_spin_mutex { void lock() noexcept { // Stage 1: Quick spin (~5 iterations, ~25ns) // Stage 2: CPU pause instructions (~10 iterations, ~400ns) // Stage 3: Extended pause (~3000 iterations, ~1ms) // Stage 4: Yield once, then back to stage 3 }
bool try_lock() noexcept { return !flag.test_and_set(std::memory_order_acquire); }
void unlock() noexcept { flag.clear(std::memory_order_release); }
private: std::atomic_flag flag = ATOMIC_FLAG_INIT; }; ```
**Key principle**: The audio thread should only ever call `try_lock()` and fall back to an alternative strategy on failure. The `lock()` method with waiting runs on non-audio threads.
---
### 4. **DSP Pipeline Best Practices (2026 Overview)**
**Real-time constraints:** - Voice calls: ~20-40 ms end-to-end latency budget - Interactive instruments: single-digit milliseconds - ANC/Assistive listening: < 10-15 ms
**Common failure modes:** 1. Hidden sample-rate changes at runtime 2. Float64 vs fixed-point numerics differences 3. Latency creep from adding "safety buffers" 4. Evaluating on wrong data (quiet office vs real-world) 5. Over-smoothing before integration
---
### 5. **General Real-Time Safety Rules**
The **golden rule**: *"Thou shalt not call time-unbounded operations in your real-time thread."*
**What to avoid:** - Memory allocation (`malloc`, `new`) - System calls - I/O operations - Mutex locks - Any operation with unbounded execution time
**What to use instead:** - `std::atomic` for simple parameters - Lock-free SPSC FIFOs (`boost::spsc_queue`) for message streams - Immutable data structures for complex state - Pre-allocated buffers
---
## Summary Recommendations
| Scenario | Solution | |----------|----------| | Single parameter sharing | `std::atomic<T>` with release/acquire | | Message streams | Lock-free SPSC FIFO | | Complex data structures | Immutable data structures (copy-on-write) | | Must use locks | `audio_spin_mutex` with back-off (audio thread: try_lock only) | | Compile-time safety | Clang's new Performance Constraints | | Runtime detection | RealtimeSanitizer (RTSan) |
These resources represent the cutting-edge of real-time audio safety as of 2024-2025, with practical implementations you can adopt immediately.

## Main Results
### 1. Four Common Mistakes in Audio Development **Source:** ataStypixel Blog by Michael Tyson
**Four Cardinal Rules:** 1. **Don't hold locks on the audio thread** - Causes priority inversion and glitches 2. **Don't use Objective-C/Swift on the audio thread** - These languages hold locks internally during normal operations 3. **Don't allocate memory on the audio thread** - Unbounded execution time can cause dropouts 4. **Don't do file or network IO on the audio thread** - Also has unbounded execution time
**Key Issues:** - Violating these rules causes audio glitches, clicks, and crackles - Priority inversion can occur when higher-priority threads wait on lower-priority ones - Objective-C method calls and property accesses hold locks internally - Memory allocation functions like `malloc()` use locks and have unpredictable timing

Discussion about common errors in audio plugin development in the JUCE framework community.

**Common Pitfalls:** - Disrupting the event queue during processing - Improper reset implementation - Incorrect plugin composition - Issues with variable-size signals - Parameter initialization order dependencies
### 4. Plugin Development Checklist **Source:** robotplanet.dk by Joachim Michaelis
**Essential Tests:** - Test both stereo and mono input/output - Random parameter stress testing (20-50 times) - Test multiple sample rates (22050, 44100, 96000 Hz) - Send digital silence and check for CPU spikes - Send very low signals (-100 dB) and check CPU - Send loud spikes (+100 dB) and check for noise bursts - Check for DC offset with extreme settings - Test with short ASIO buffer sizes - Run 24-hour duration tests - Test multiple instances simultaneously - Test preset save/load functionality - Test multiple DAWs (hosts) - Test MIDI message handling - Have others test your plugin
### 5. Debugging Audio Units with auvaltool **Source:** Moonbase.sh by Sudara
**Key Points:** - Use `auvaltool` (or `pluginval`) to validate Audio Unit plugins - Audio Units must pass validation to appear in DAWs like Logic Pro - Common error code: 4099 (check audio/midi inputs/outputs match registration type) - Debugging requires either using x86_64 binary or disabling SIP - System registry issues can prevent plugins from appearing

## SmoothedValue Overview
**`juce::SmoothedValue`** is a utility class designed specifically for smoothing parameter changes in real-time audio processing to avoid glitches. Key thread-safety characteristics:
### Thread-Safe Design Patterns
1. **Lock-free operations**: All methods are marked `noexcept`, making them safe for the audio thread: - `setTargetValue()` - Set the target value from any thread - `getNextValue()` - Get the next smoothed value on the audio thread - `reset()` - Configure ramp parameters
2. **No allocations**: The class only contains primitive types (`FloatType`, `int countdown`) - no dynamic memory allocation occurs during operation.
### Typical Usage Pattern
```cpp // In your audio processor: SmoothedValue<float> gain;
// In prepareToPlay() (not audio thread): gain.reset(sampleRate, 0.02); // 20ms ramp
// From UI/thread parameter changes: gain.setTargetValue(newGainValue); // Thread-safe, lock-free
// In processBlock() (audio thread): for (int i = 0; i < numSamples; ++i) { float smoothedGain = gain.getNextValue(); // Use smoothedGain... } ```
### Key Features for Audio Thread Safety
| Feature | Purpose | |---------|---------| | `noexcept` methods | Guarantees no exceptions on audio thread | | No heap allocation | Prevents audio thread allocation issues | | Atomic-like semantics | Simple primitive values can be safely read/written from different threads | | `Linear` vs `Multiplicative` smoothing | Choose based on parameter type (linear for most, multiplicative for dB/frequency) |
### Related: AudioProcessorValueTreeState Thread Safety

I found several comprehensive resources on psychedelic ambient/psybient sound design techniques. Here's a synthesis of the key information:
## Advanced Sound Design Techniques for Psybient/Ambient
### 1. **Granular Synthesis & Textural Freezing** - Load any audio sample into a granular processor and "freeze" it on a single position - Use long grain sizes (200-800ms) with high density for smooth, smeared textures - Add small amounts of "jitter" or "spray" to make sounds feel alive and non-repeating - Tools: Output Portal, Arturia eFX Fragments, Omnisphere, Pigments
### 2. **Asynchronous Modulation (Conflicting Cycles)** - Use multiple LFOs and looping envelopes at different, unsynced rates - Example: LFO 1 at 0.07 Hz (14-sec cycle), LFO 2 at 0.13 Hz (7.7-sec cycle), looping envelope at 15-sec cycle - This creates sounds that evolve naturally and almost never repeat the same way - Essential for avoiding predictable "whoosh-whoosh" patterns
### 3. **Recursive Reverb & Drone Mining** - Use creative reverbs that feed their own reflections back into the algorithm - Excavate hidden harmonic overtones from simple source material - Tools: MYON, Valhalla Shimmer, or similar "freeze" capable reverbs
### 4. **No-Input Feedback Drones** - Create feedback loops in your DAW by routing an aux track back into itself - "Play" the resulting self-oscillation with EQs and effects - **Caution:** Use a limiter on master bus to prevent hearing/speaker damage
### 5. **Harmonic Layering with Saturation** - Use saturation and clipping as synthesis tools to create new harmonics - Soft clipping adds warm even-order harmonics; hard clipping adds aggressive odd-order harmonics - Great for bringing life to dark, low-passed pads
### 6. **Worldizing & Acoustic Re-amping** - Play sounds through speakers in real physical spaces and re-record - The "Murch 4x Method": Speed up 4x, record acoustically, slow back down for impossibly vast organic reverb
### 7. **Textural Glitch & Subtle Imperfection** - Use glitch plugins at very low mix (10%) for surface texture - Add micro-edits, random grains, and pitch shifts for "beautiful damage" - Makes digital sounds feel more organic and tangible
## Key Synthesizer Recommendations
From the **Bluetech interview**, notable hardware/software includes: - **Modular synthesis** - Eurorack systems for hands-on exploration - **Intellijel Atlantis** (SH-101 clone) - frequently used - **Synthesis Technologies E352 Cloud Terrarium** - for complex textures - **Empress Reverb pedal** - for lush infinite space - **KARP Odyssey** - for live performances - **Abtrakt Avalon** - TB-303 style for acid elements
## Core Psybient Characteristics
- **Tempo:** 60-100 BPM (much slower than psytrance) - **Atmospheric soundscapes** with layered synthesizers and organic instruments - **Ethnic/world influences** - flutes, tribal sounds, field recordings - **Slow, evolving textures** rather than aggressive peaks - **Spiritual/meditative** focus for introspection
## Workflow Tips
1. Start with **characterful source material** (piano chords, guitar feedback, vocal phrases) 2. Combine techniques: worldize → granular freeze → recursive reverb → asynchronous modulation 3. **Control low-end** with high-pass filters; use separate clean sub-bass for foundation 4. **Check mono compatibility** frequently to avoid phase issues

{
  "file_path": "/home/myuser/playbooks/vst-product-lifecycle-playbook/research/domain-analysis.md",
  "content": "# Domain Analysis — VST Plugin Development & Commercial Release

## Executive Summary

The VST (Virtual Studio Technology) plugin market is a $1.45 billion industry (2023) projected to reach $2.87 billion by 2030. This domain covers software audio processing tools that integrate with Digital Audio Workstations (DAWs). The full lifecycle spans: concept → research → DSP implementation → UI design → testing → licensing → marketplace listing → marketing → sales.

---

## Standard Processes

### Development Lifecycle

| Phase | Activities | Duration |
|-------|------------|----------|
| **Concept & Research** | Sound design research, competitive analysis, feature definition | 1-4 weeks |
| **DSP Implementation** | Audio processing algorithms, synthesis engines, effects processing | 2-8 weeks |
| **UI/UX Design** | Control layout, visual design, preset management UI | 2-4 weeks |
| **Testing** | Unit tests, DAW compatibility, audio thread safety, user testing | 1-3 weeks |
| **Licensing Integration** | Copy protection, license validation, activation workflow | 1-2 weeks |
| **Release** | Build for multiple platforms, installer creation, marketplace submission | 1-2 weeks |
| **Marketing & Sales** | Pre-launch, launch, post-launch campaigns | Ongoing |

### Technical Stack (Standard)

| Component | Standard Choice | Alternatives |
|-----------|----------------|--------------|
| Framework | JUCE 8.0.x | iPlug2, Qt, Custom |
| Language | C++17 | C++20, Rust (experimental) |
| Build System | CMake 3.22+ | Projucer (JUCE-only) |
| Plugin Formats | VST3, AU, AAX | LV2, CLAP |
| Testing DAW | Multiple | REAPER, Ableton, Logic, Pro Tools |
| Dependency Mgmt | FetchContent | Git Submodules, Conan |

---

## Common Failure Modes

### Development Failures

| Failure Mode | Description | Prevention |
|--------------|-------------|-------------|
| **Audio Thread Allocation** | `malloc`/`new` in `processBlock()` | Pre-allocate in `prepareToPlay()` |
| **Priority Inversion** | Mutex locks blocking audio thread | Use lock-free queues, atomics |
| **Unbounded Execution** | Non-deterministic operations in RT context | RealtimeSanitizer, code review |
| **Parameter Smoothing Glitches** | Stepped parameter changes cause clicks | `SmoothedValue` for all parameters |
| **DC Offset** | Accumulating DC in filters or feedback paths | High-pass filters, DC blocking |
| **Gain Staging Issues** | Clipping or excessive headroom loss | Conservative gain staging, metering |
| **Thread Safety Violations** | Shared state without synchronization | `std::atomic`, SPSC queues, immutable data |
| **State Serialization Bugs** | Presets don't load correctly, crash on load | APVTS patterns, thorough testing |

### Release Failures

| Failure Mode | Description | Prevention |
|--------------|-------------|-------------|
| **DAW Compatibility** | Works in one DAW, fails in another | Test in 3+ DAWs, use auval/pluginval |
| **Platform Differences** | Mac/Windows/Linux behavior differs | Platform-specific testing |
| **Licensing System Failure** | Legitimate users locked out | Fallback modes, offline activation |
| **Marketplace Rejection** | Missing icons, descriptions, permissions | Follow submission checklists |
| **Piracy** | Cracked versions within days of release | Multi-layer protection, online activation |

### Marketing Failures

| Failure Mode | Description | Prevention |
|--------------|-------------|-------------|
| **No Audience Before Launch** | Launching to 0 interest | Build waitlist, community engagement |
| **Generic Messaging** | "Great plugin for producers" | Specific value proposition, demo content |
| **Wrong Price Point** | Too expensive for indie market, too cheap to sustain | Competitor analysis, tier strategy |
| **No Differentiation** | "Another synth" in saturated market | Clear unique value, sound demos |

---

## Terminology Glossary

### Audio Processing

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| **DSP** | Digital Signal Processing — algorithmic manipulation of audio |
| **RT Context** | Real-time context — audio thread with strict timing constraints |
| **Sample Rate** | Samples per second (44100, 48000, 96000 Hz common) |
| **Buffer Size** | Samples processed per callback (64, 128, 256, 512 common) |
| **Latency** | Delay through plugin, must be reported accurately |
| **DC Offset** | DC component in audio signal, causes clicks and headroom loss |

### Synthesis Types

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| **Subtractive** | Rich oscillator → filter → amp envelope |
| **FM** | Modulator frequencies affect carrier frequencies |
| **Wavetable** | Morph between stored waveforms |
| **Granular** | Break audio into grains, manipulate individually |
| **Additive** | Combine sine waves (partials) at different frequencies |
| **Physical Modeling** | Mathematical simulation of acoustic instruments |

### Plugin Architecture

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| **Processor** | Audio engine — real-time processing |
| **Controller** | UI layer — parameter display, user interaction |
| **APVTS** | AudioProcessorValueTreeState — JUCE's parameter management system |
| **ADSR** | Attack-Decay-Sustain-Release envelope |
| **LFO** | Low-Frequency Oscillator for modulation |

### Licensing & Distribution

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| **VST3** | Steinberg's plugin format (current standard) |
| **AU** | Audio Units — Apple's format |
| **AAX** | Avid Audio Extension — Pro Tools format |
| **iLok** | PACE's licensing platform (USB dongle + cloud) |
| **APVTS** | JUCE's state serialization for presets |

---

## KPIs Tracked by Professionals

| Category | KPI | Target |
|----------|-----|--------|
| **Quality** | CPU usage at 48kHz/128 samples | < 5% single core |
| **Quality** | Latency contribution | < 1ms (zero for effects) |
| **Quality** | Audio thread safety audit | 0 violations |
| **Quality** | Crash rate per 1000 sessions | < 0.1 |
| **Business** | Trial-to-paid conversion | > 5% |
| **Business** | Piracy rate (cracked vs purchased) | < 70% (optimistic) |
| **Business** | Support ticket ratio | < 2% of users |
| **Business** | Marketplace rating | > 4.0/5.0 |

---

## Regulatory & Compliance

| Requirement | Scope | Notes |
|-------------|-------|-------|
| **Code Signing** | macOS, Windows | Required for AUv3, recommended for all |
| **GDPR** | EU customers | Email collection, data handling |
| **VST3 SDK License** | Steinberg | Free for commercial use |
| **AAX SDK License** | Avid | Requires developer account |
| **Marketplace Terms** | Each platform | Review KVR, Plugin Boutique requirements |

---

## Platform-Specific Concerns

### Linux
- **Formats**: VST3, LV2, CLAP native; Windows VST via Wine/Yabridge
- **Paths**: `~/.vst3`, `~/.lv2`, `~/.clap`
- **Testing**: REAPER, Ardour, Bitwig
- **Dependencies**: libx11-xcb-dev, libxcb-*, libfontconfig, libgtkmm-3.0

### macOS
- **Formats**: AU, VST3, AAX
- **Paths**: `~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/`
- **Requirements**: Code signing, notarization
- **Testing**: Logic Pro, Ableton, REAPER

### Windows
- **Formats**: VST3, AAX
- **Paths**: `C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST3`
- **Requirements**: Code signing recommended
- **Testing**: Ableton, REAPER, Pro Tools

---

## Sources

- [VST3 Controller-Processor Communication](https://nyxfx.dev/vst3-controller-processor-communication-strategies/)
- [JUCE Forum - Release Build Best Practices](https://forum.juce.com/t/best-practices-for-building-releases-of-vst3-plugins/44598)
- [JUCE Tutorial: Package Your Plugin](https://docs.juce.com/master/tutorial_app_plugin_packaging.html)
- [Audio Plugin Industry Statistics 2026](https://gitnux.org/audio-plugin-industry-statistics/)
- [PACE Anti-Piracy Platform](https://www.paceap.com/proaudio.html)
- [VST Licensing Guide - MuseHub](https://blog.musehub.com/vst-plugins-licensing-protection/)
- [LLVM Real-Time Safety Revolution - ADC 2024](https://conference.audio.dev/llvms-real-time-safety-revolution-tools-for-modern-audio-development-adc-2024/)
- [Memory Ordering in Audio - Bruce Dawson](https://www.bruce.audio/post/2025/02/24/memory_ordering/)
- [Locks in Real-Time Audio - Timur Audio](https://timur.audio/using-locks-in-real-time-audio-processing-safely)
- [Common Audio Development Mistakes - A Tasty Pixel](https://atastypixel.com/four-common-mistakes-in-audio-development/)
- [Plugin Development Checklist](https://robotplanet.dk/audio/plugin_development_checklist)

---

*Created: Phase 1 — Domain Research*"
}

{
  "file_path": "/home/myuser/playbooks/vst-product-lifecycle-playbook/research/best-practices.md",
  "content": "# Best Practices — VST Plugin Development & Commercial Release

## Development Best Practices

### Audio Thread Safety (Critical)

| Practice | Rationale | Implementation |
|----------|-----------|----------------|
| **No allocations in processBlock()** | `malloc`/`new` have unbounded execution time | Pre-allocate all buffers in `prepareToPlay()` |
| **No mutex locks on audio thread** | Priority inversion causes glitches | Use `std::atomic` for simple params, lock-free SPSC queues for messages |
| **No system calls** | File/network I/O blocks indefinitely | Offload to worker threads |
| **No Objective-C/Swift on audio thread** | These languages hold locks internally | Use pure C++ in RT path |

**Real-time Safety Pattern:**
```cpp
// WRONG - allocation in processBlock
void processBlock(AudioBuffer<float>& buffer, MidiBuffer&) {
    std::vector<float> temp(buffer.getNumSamples()); // ALLOCATES!
    // ...
}

// RIGHT - pre-allocated
class Processor {
    std::vector<float> tempBuffer;
    void prepareToPlay(double sr, int bs) {
        tempBuffer.resize(bs); // Pre-allocate
    }
    void processBlock(AudioBuffer<float>& buffer, MidiBuffer&) {
        // Use pre-allocated buffer
    }
};
```

**Sources:** [LLVM Real-Time Safety Revolution - ADC 2024](https://conference.audio.dev/llvms-real-time-safety-revolution-tools-for-modern-audio-development-adc-2024/), [Common Audio Development Mistakes - A Tasty Pixel](https://atastypixel.com/four-common-mistakes-in-audio-development/)

---

### Parameter Management (APVTS Pattern)

| Practice | Pattern | Notes |
|----------|---------|-------|
| **Central parameter state** | `AudioProcessorValueTreeState` | Single source of truth for all parameters |
| **Thread-safe access** | `getRawParameterValue()` returns `std::atomic<float>*` | Safe to read from audio thread |
| **UI binding** | `SliderAttachment`, `ButtonAttachment` | Automatic bidirectional sync |
| **State serialization** | XML via `getStateInformation()`/`setStateInformation()` | Presets, DAW session save |

**Sources:** [JUCE APVTS Tutorial](https://docs.juce.com/master/tutorial_audio_processor_value_tree_state.html), [JUCE Forum - APVTS Design Pattern](https://forum.juce.com/t/apvts-design-pattern-review/65536)

---

### Parameter Smoothing

| Practice | When | Implementation |
|----------|------|----------------|
| **Always smooth parameter changes** | Every continuous parameter | `SmoothedValue<float>` with 20-50ms ramp |
| **Linear vs Multiplicative** | Linear for most, multiplicative for dB/frequency | `SmoothedValue<float, SmoothedValue<float>::Multiplicative>` |

**Pattern:**
```cpp
// In prepareToPlay
gain.reset(sampleRate, 0.02); // 20ms smoothing

// When parameter changes (any thread)
gain.setTargetValue(newGain);

// In processBlock (audio thread)
for (int i = 0; i < numSamples; ++i) {
    float g = gain.getNextValue();
    output[i] = input[i] * g;
}
```

**Source:** [JUCE SmoothedValue Documentation](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1SmoothedValue.html)

---

### Gain Staging

| Practice | Target | Reasoning |
|----------|--------|-----------|
| **Input normalization** | -12 to -6 dBFS peak | Conservative headroom for processing |
| **Inter-stage headroom** | Keep 6-12 dB headroom | Cascading effects accumulate |
| **Output normalization** | -6 to -3 dBFS peak | Prevents clipping in DAW |
| **Metering** | Visual feedback on all stages | Users need visibility |

**Sources:** Standard audio engineering practice, validated across plugin development forums.

---

### Build & Distribution

| Practice | Implementation |
|----------|----------------|
| **CMake with FetchContent** | Self-contained, reproducible builds |
| **Debug vs Release builds** | Debug for development, Release for distribution |
| **Multiple format targets** | Build VST3 + AU (Mac) + AAX simultaneously |
| **Installer creation** | Inno Setup (Windows), Packages (macOS), scripts (Linux) |
| **Code signing** | Required for AUv3, recommended for all platforms |

**Source:** [JUCE Plugin Packaging Tutorial](https://docs.juce.com/master/tutorial_app_plugin_packaging.html)

---

## Sound Design Best Practices

### Synthesis Type Selection

| Need | Best Type | Reason |
|------|-----------|--------|
| Classic analog tones | Subtractive | Familiar, warm, controllable |
| Metallic/bell tones | FM | Complex inharmonic spectra |
| Evolving/modern textures | Wavetable | Morphing creates movement |
| Atmospheric/pads | Granular | Transforms any audio into textures |
| Physical instruments | Physical modeling | Realistic attack/decay behavior |

**Sources:** [Types of Synthesis - LANDR](https://blog.landr.com/types-of-synthesis), [10+ Synthesis Types - Unison](https://unison.audio/synthesis-types/)

---

### Psychedelic/Ambient/Psybient Techniques

| Technique | Application |
|-----------|-------------|
| **Asynchronous modulation** | Multiple LFOs at unsynced rates (e.g., 0.07 Hz, 0.13 Hz, 15-sec envelope) creates ever-evolving textures |
| **Granular freezing** | Hold single position, add jitter/spray for organic variation |
| **Recursive reverb** | Feedback reverb into itself, mine harmonics from simple sources |
| **Worldizing** | Play through speakers in physical space, re-record |
| **Layered saturation** | Add harmonics to dark pads, soft clipping for warmth |
| **Conflicting cycles** | LFO rates at prime ratios (7, 11, 13) prevent repetition |

**Sources:** [Ambient Sound Design - Artists in DSP](https://artistsindsp.com/ambient-sound-design-7-advanced-techniques-for-evolving-drones-and-textures/), [Bluetech Interview - Psybient.org](https://www.psybient.org/love/bluetech-interview/)

---

## UI/UX Best Practices

### Control Selection

| Control Type | Use Case | Pros/Cons |
|--------------|----------|-----------|
| **Knobs** | Continuous parameters, space-efficient | Compact, but circular motion less intuitive for mouse |
| **Sliders/Faders** | Level comparison, precise values | Good visibility, but take more space |
| **Meters** | Visual feedback, levels | Essential for gain staging |
| **Switches/Buttons** | Discrete options | Clear on/off states |

**Design Guidelines:**
- Touch targets: Minimum 44x44px for accessibility
- Visual feedback: Immediate response to user action
- Consistent sizing: Related controls should be visually grouped
- High contrast: Visible in all lighting conditions

**Sources:** [UX Patterns in Synthesizer Plugins - Voger Design](https://vogerdesign.com/blog/basic-ux-patterns-in-the-development-of-synthesizer-plugins-awesome/), [Slider UI Design - Setproduct](https://setproduct.com/blog/slider-ui-design)

---

### Accessibility

| Practice | Implementation |
|----------|----------------|
| **Keyboard navigation** | Arrow keys for value changes, Tab between controls |
| **Screen reader support** | ARIA labels, accessible descriptions |
| **High contrast mode** | Alternative color schemes for visibility |
| **Automation** | All parameters exposed to DAW automation |

---

## Commercial Best Practices

### Licensing Strategy

| Solution | Pros | Cons | Best For |
|----------|------|------|----------|
| **PACE iLok** | Industry standard, robust, trusted | Expensive, complex, dongle can frustrate users | Established developers, high-value plugins |
| **MuseHub DRM** | Easy implementation, integrated distribution | Newer platform, less proven | Smaller developers, quick to market |
| **Cryptlex** | Modern, cloud-based, analytics | Newer player, cost considerations | SaaS-style licensing |
| **Custom/Proprietary** | Full control, no dependency | Security risks, maintenance burden | Developers with security expertise |
| **Serial numbers only** | Simple implementation | Easily pirated | Low-risk, low-value products |

**Sources:** [PACE Anti-Piracy](https://www.paceap.com/proaudio.html), [VST Licensing Guide - MuseHub](https://blog.musehub.com/vst-plugins-licensing-protection/)

---

### Marketplace Strategy

| Platform | Strengths | Audience | Cost |
|----------|-----------|----------|------|
| **KVR Audio** | Largest community, reviews, forums | Producers, hobbyists | Free listing, commission on sales |
| **Plugin Boutique** | Strong marketing, bundles | Professional producers | Commission model |
| **Direct sales** | Full control, no commission | Established audience | Payment processing fees |

**2026 Trends:**
- Subscription models: 45% of plugin revenue
- AI-powered plugins: $250M market (35% YoY growth)
- Indie developers: 15% market share
- Black Friday sales: 300% YoY increase

**Source:** [Audio Plugin Industry Statistics 2026](https://gitnux.org/audio-plugin-industry-statistics/)

---

### Pricing Strategy

| Approach | Example | Psychology |
|----------|---------|------------|
| **Tiered pricing** | $29 basic, $79 pro, $149 suite | Capture different budgets |
| **Introductory pricing** | 50% off launch week | Creates urgency |
| **Perpetual + upgrade** | $99 purchase, $49 major upgrades | Recurring revenue |
| **Subscription** | $9.99/month | Predictable revenue, lower barrier |

**Key Insight:** Even $9/month validates your go-to-market faster than 10,000 free users who never convert.

**Source:** [Indie App Marketing Strategies 2026](https://rapidappstore.com/blog/indie-app-marketing-strategies)

---

### Marketing for Solo Developers

| Activity | Time | Impact |
|----------|------|--------|
| **Community engagement** | 30 min/day | First 20 customers |
| **Content marketing (SEO)** | 4 hrs/week | Traffic in 2-3 months |
| **Build in public** | 15 min/day | Brand awareness + network |
| **Product Hunt launch** | 1 day prep | Spike of 100+ signups |

**Golden Rule:** "Build for the community, not the algorithm. 10 credible conversations beat 100,000 views."

**Source:** [Indie App Marketing Strategies 2026](https://rapidappstore.com/blog/indie-app-marketing-strategies)

---

## Testing Best Practices

| Test Type | Implementation |
|-----------|----------------|
| **DAW compatibility** | Test in 3+ DAWs (REAPER, Ableton, Logic/Bitwig) |
| **Sample rate testing** | Test at 22050, 44100, 48000, 96000 Hz |
| **Buffer size testing** | Test at 64, 128, 256, 512 samples |
| **Parameter stress** | Random parameter changes 20-50 times |
| **DC offset check** | Extreme settings, verify no DC accumulation |
| **24-hour test** | Run overnight, check for leaks, crashes |
| **Multiple instances** | 8+ instances simultaneously |
| **Preset save/load** | Round-trip all presets |

**Source:** [Plugin Development Checklist](https://robotplanet.dk/audio/plugin_development_checklist)

---

*Created: Phase 1 — Domain Research*"
}

  "content": "# Competitive Playbook Audit — VST Development Playbooks

## Executive Summary

Multiple VST development playbooks exist in the system. Per scope decision, **none are integrated** — this playbook is standalone to test the playbook-creator-playbook system independently. However, an audit of their structure provides insight into what a VST playbook typically covers.

---

## Existing Playbooks Identified

| Playbook | Location | Focus |

| VST Plugin Playbook v7 Unified | `~/agents/juce-agent/playbooks/vst-plugin-playbook-v7-unified.json` | DSP implementation, 13 phases |
| JUCE VST Development Playbook v3 | `~/Documents/playbookdata/juce-vst-dev-playbook-v3.json` | Earlier iteration |
| VST Plugin Playbook v5 | `~/agents/juce-agent/playbooks/vst-plugin-playbook-v5.json` | Earlier iteration |

---

## Audit: VST Plugin Playbook v7 Unified

### What It Covers Well (KEEP)
- **DSP implementation phases** — Detailed task breakdown for audio processing
- **Audio thread safety** — Explicit failure modes and prevention
- **Parameter management** — APVTS patterns, smoothing, state
- **DAW testing** — Human perceptual testing phase
- **Knowledge base structure** — Technical KB with sound design bridge

### What It Misses (ADD for this playbook)
- **Commercial phases** — No licensing, marketplace, pricing, marketing
- **Business strategy** — No go-to-market, customer acquisition
- **Post-release** — No continuous improvement, analytics
- **Sound design methodology** — KB structure but not methodology

### What Contradicts Current Strategy (REMOVE)
- **No contradiction** — Different scope, not conflicting

### Structure Analysis
- 13 phases, detailed task breakdown per phase
- Strong gate conditions with verification
- Role-based (single agent)
- Knowledge base integration

---

## Gap Analysis: What This Playbook Adds

| Category | Existing Coverage | This Playbook Adds |
|----------|------------------|-------------------|
| **DSP Development** | ✅ Comprehensive | Inherit approach |
| **Sound Design KB** | ⚠️ Bridge exists, methodology missing | Full methodology, genre-specific |
| **UI/UX** | ⚠️ Mentioned | Full design phase |
| **Commercial/Licensing** | ❌ Not covered | Full licensing integration phase |
| **Marketplace Strategy** | ❌ Not covered | KVR, Plugin Boutique, direct sales |
| **Marketing** | ❌ Not covered | Solo developer achievable strategy |
| **Pricing** | ❌ Not covered | Tiered, subscription, perpetual analysis |
| **Post-Release** | ❌ Not covered | Analytics, updates, continuous improvement |
| **Testing** | ✅ DAW testing phase | Inherit + expand |

---

## Structural Differences

| Aspect | Existing Playbook | This Playbook |
|--------|------------------|---------------|
| **Phases** | 13 | 16+ (including commercial) |
| **Role Model** | role-based-single-agent | role-based-single-agent |
| **KB Architecture** | Technical + Sound Design bridge | 5-layer (Technical, Sound Design, UI/UX, Commercial, Reference) |
| **Target Audience** | C++ beginners with AI assistance | Same audience, broader scope |
| **End Goal** | Working VST3 plugin | Working VST3 plugin + commercial viability |

---

## Lessons Learned from Existing Playbooks

### Strengths to Incorporate
1. **Gate verification format** — Explicit PASS/FAIL with evidence
2. **Audio thread safety phase** — Dedicated safety audit phase
3. **Sound design bridge** — Translation from descriptors to DSP parameters
4. **DAW testing phase** — Human perceptual testing, not just unit tests

### Gaps to Address
1. **Commercial viability** — Products must sell, not just work
2. **Market positioning** — Saturated market requires differentiation
3. **Solo developer constraints** — Marketing achievable without team
4. **Knowledge depth** — Bridged knowledge needs explicit layer structure

---

## Integration Decision

**Decision:** None of the existing playbooks are integrated. This playbook:
- Uses the playbook-creator-playbook system from scratch
- Covers full product lifecycle (development + commercial)
- Tests PBCPB system independently
- Maintains separate 5-layer KB architecture

**Rationale:** The commission brief explicitly requested testing the playbook-creator-playbook system. Integration with existing VST playbooks would confound that test. Additionally, the existing playbooks lack commercial phases, requiring new content regardless.

---

*Created: Phase 1 — Domain Research*"
}

{
  "file_path": "/home/myuser/playbooks/vst-product-lifecycle-playbook/research/sme-interviews.md",
  "content": "# Subject Matter Expert Interviews — Self-Interview

## Methodology

The commissioning user is the domain expert (single developer using AI assistance for VST development). This document captures institutional knowledge from their experience and requirements.

**Interview methodology:** Structured self-interview based on the user's commission brief and project context.

---

## Interview: Target User (Solo Developer + AI Assistance)

### The Actual Process

**Q: What does the real VST development process look like, versus what's documented?**

A: The documented process assumes linear progression: design → implement → test → release. In practice:
- **Iterative discovery:** Sound design research often changes DSP approach mid-implementation
- **AI-assisted coding:** Multiple Claude Code sessions per feature, hitting token limits, resuming
- **Platform friction:** Linux-specific issues (dependency hell, DAW differences) consume unexpected time
- **Testing reality:** REAPER is primary DAW, but users report issues from other DAWs

**Q: What steps aren't written down?**

A:
- Gain staging is discovered through audio issues, not designed upfront
- Parameter smoothing is often retrofitted after hearing clicks
- Preset creation happens after "sound design passes" that aren't formalized
- Marketing begins before the plugin is finished (build anticipation)
- Licensing decision is usually deferred until "the plugin works"

**Q: What commonly goes wrong?**

A:
- **Audio thread allocations** — Hardest bug to find, causes random glitches
- **State serialization** — Presets that don't load, or crash on load
- **DAW compatibility** — Works in REAPER, fails in Ableton
- **Scope creep** — "One more feature" delays release indefinitely
- **Market invisibility** — Launch to crickets, no pre-launch audience

**Q: What decisions require judgment versus always-the-same?**

A:

| Always-the-Same | Requires Judgment |
|----------------|-------------------|
| Audio thread safety rules | Sound identity (warm vs bright) |
| APVTS parameter pattern | UI aesthetic direction |
| Build configuration | Feature scope vs timeline |
| CMake + FetchContent | Pricing level |
| Unit test framework | Marketing channels |
| SmoothedValue for params | Genre focus for sound design |

**Q: What do you wish you'd known before your first plugin build?**

A:
1. **Gain staging matters from day one** — Retrofitting is painful
2. **Test in multiple DAWs early** — Not just your primary DAW
3. **Preset system design upfront** — Not as afterthought
4. **Audio thread safety is not optional** — Random glitches destroy reputation
5. **Marketing starts before release** — Build audience during development
6. **Scope ruthlessly** — First plugin doesn't need every feature
7. **Licensing is complex** — Start simple, add protection later

---

## Interview: Sound Design Knowledge

### Unwritten Sound Design Process

**Q: How do you approach sound design for a new plugin?**

A: The process isn't formalized but goes:
1. **Genre target:** "This is for psybient/ambient" sets constraints
2. **Sound identity words:** "Warm, evolving, atmospheric" → parameter ranges
3. **Reference sounds:** Listen to existing plugins in the genre
4. **DSP experiments:** Quick prototypes, not production code
5. **Preset creation:** Dial in sounds that showcase the plugin
6. **Iteration:** Users hear things I didn't intend, adjust

**Q: What's the relationship between sound design words and DSP parameters?**

A: This is the gap. "Warm" could mean:
- Low-pass filter cutoff 200-800 Hz
- Subtle saturation (even harmonics)
- Slight pitch drift (analog drift emulation)
- Slower attack envelopes

The bridge isn't automatic — requires knowledge of both sound design vocabulary and DSP implementation.

**Q: What genre-specific knowledge matters?**

A:

| Genre | Key Characteristics | DSP Implications |
|-------|---------------------|------------------|
| **Psybient** | Slow evolving textures, 60-100 BPM, ethnic elements | Long LFO cycles, granular processing, worldizing |
| **Ambient** | No percussion focus, atmospheric | Reverb-heavy, slow modulation, low-pass filters |
| **Psychedelic** | Unpredictable, experimental | Asynchronous modulation, glitch effects, feedback |
| **Pad** | Sustained, harmonic, evolving | Slow LFOs, detuning, filter envelopes |
| **Creative** | Unique, non-standard | Whatever produces interesting results |

---

## Interview: Commercial Viability

**Q: What makes a plugin commercially successful?**

A:

| Factor | Impact |
|--------|--------|
| **Unique sound** | Differentiation in saturated market |
| **Reasonable price** | $20-80 sweet spot for indie |
| **Professional presets** | Users want instant gratification |
| **Video demos** | Audio demos alone don't sell |
| **Community engagement** | Build audience before launch |
| **Platform coverage** | Mac + Windows minimum, Linux bonus |

**Q: What marketing is achievable by a solo developer?**

A:
- **Content marketing:** Blog posts, YouTube tutorials — time-intensive but free
- **Community engagement:** Reddit, Discord, forums — 30 min/day
- **Product Hunt launch:** One-day spike in visibility
- **Plugin directory listings:** KVR, Plugin Boutique — free
- **Email list:** Build during development, launch to list
- **NOT achievable without budget:** Paid ads, influencer campaigns, PR firms

**Q: What licensing approach is practical?**

A:

| Approach | Practicality |
|----------|--------------|
| **No protection** | Too easy to pirate, but low friction |
| **Serial number** | Simple but easily cracked |
| **Online activation** | Balance of security and UX |
| **iLok/PACE** | Professional but expensive, user friction |
| **Custom solution** | High development cost, security risk |

**Recommendation for indie:** Start with online activation, simple implementation, reasonable security. Add hardware dongle support only if piracy becomes existential threat.

---

## Interview: Technical Constraints

**Q: What Linux-specific issues should the playbook address?**

A:
- **Dependencies:** libx11-xcb-dev, libxcb-*, libfontconfig, libgtkmm-3.0 — not documented in one place
- **REAPER quirks:** Plugin paths differ from system paths
- **Windows plugins:** Yabridge required, adds complexity
- **Testing limitation:** Fewer Linux DAW options for compatibility testing
- **Distribution:** Linux users expect native builds, not Wine wrappers

**Q: What JUCE patterns are essential?**

A:
- **APVTS** — AudioProcessorValueTreeState for all parameters
- **SmoothedValue** — Every continuous parameter
- **processBlock()** — No allocations, no locks, no system calls
- **prepareToPlay()** — All pre-allocation
- **getStateInformation/setStateInformation** — Presets and DAW save
- **Editor/Processor separation** — UI never touches audio thread

**Q: What C++ level is expected?**

A:
- **Knows:** Python/JavaScript, basic C++ theory
- **Learning:** JUCE framework, DSP implementation
- **Needs from playbook:** C++ curated for audio relevance, not general C++ tutorial
- **AI assistance:** Handles implementation details, but needs direction

---

## Synthesis: Key Insights

1. **Process is iterative, not linear** — Sound design research changes implementation
2. **AI assistance is the norm** — Multiple sessions, token limits expected
3. **Linux is underserved** — Documentation gap for Linux-specific issues
4. **Marketing starts during development** — Not after release
5. **Commercial viability requires planning** — Not an afterthought
6. **Sound design vocabulary ↔ DSP translation** — This bridge is the creative core
7. **Testing in multiple DAWs is essential** — REAPER alone is insufficient
8. **Licensing decision is strategic** — Affects both development and user experience

---

*Created: Phase 1 — Domain Research*"
}

{
  "file_path": "/home/myuser/playbooks/vst-product-lifecycle-playbook/research/cross-cutting-concerns.md",
  "content": "# Cross-Cutting Concerns — VST Plugin Development Playbook

## Overview

Cross-cutting concerns are requirements that apply across ALL phases of the playbook, not just to specific phases. These must be woven throughout the playbook structure.

---

## CCC-01: Audio Thread Safety

**Definition:** No audio thread violation may exist in any phase output. Violations cause unpredictable glitches that destroy user trust.

**Applies to phases:** 4 (DSP Implementation), 7 (UI), 8 (Validation), 9 (DAW Testing)

**Verification method:**
- Code review for allocations, locks, system calls
- Automated audit (e.g., RealtimeSanitizer when available)
- Stress testing with small buffer sizes (64 samples)

**Enforcement:**
- Phase 4: Audio thread audit task
- Phase 8: Unit tests for thread safety
- Phase 9: DAW testing with CPU monitoring

**Failure modes prevented:**
- FM-01: Allocation in processBlock()
- FM-02: Mutex lock on audio thread
- FM-03: Unbounded execution time

---

## CCC-02: Gain Staging

**Definition:** Every audio processing stage maintains conservative headroom (-6 to -12 dBFS). Gain staging is designed upfront, not retrofitted.

**Applies to phases:** 0 (Specification), 4 (DSP Implementation), 9 (DAW Testing)

**Verification method:**
- Specification includes gain staging plan
- Metering on all major stages
- Testing with extreme input levels
- No clipping with +6 dB input

**Enforcement:**
- Phase 0: Gain staging plan in specification
- Phase 4: Gain staging implemented with meters
- Phase 9: Perceptual testing with extreme input

---

## CCC-03: Parameter Smoothing

**Definition:** All continuous parameters use smoothing (20-50ms ramp) to prevent clicks and zipper noise.

**Applies to phases:** 4 (DSP Implementation), 8 (Validation)

**Verification method:**
- Code review: all continuous params use SmoothedValue
- Audio testing: parameter changes during audio produce no clicks
- Stress testing: rapid parameter automation

**Enforcement:**
- Phase 4: SmoothedValue for all continuous parameters
- Phase 8: Automation stress test

---

## CCC-04: DAW Compatibility

**Definition:** Plugin works correctly in multiple DAWs, not just the development DAW.

**Applies to phases:** 9 (DAW Testing), 14 (Release)

**Target DAWs:**
- **Primary:** REAPER (Linux development platform)
- **Secondary:** Ableton Live, Bitwig Studio
- **Tertiary:** Logic Pro (Mac), Pro Tools (AAX)

**Verification method:**
- Test in at least 2 DAWs before release
- Verify preset save/load in each DAW
- Verify automation recording/playback

**Enforcement:**
- Phase 9: Multi-DAW testing checklist
- Phase 14: Compatibility matrix in release notes

---

## CCC-05: State Serialization

**Definition:** Plugin state (parameters, presets, UI state) serializes correctly and loads identically.

**Applies to phases:** 4 (DSP Implementation), 5 (State Management), 8 (Validation), 9 (DAW Testing)

**Verification method:**
- Round-trip all presets (save → load → compare)
- DAW session save/load test
- Version compatibility (old presets load in new version)

**Enforcement:**
- Phase 5: State serialization implementation
- Phase 8: Preset round-trip tests
- Phase 9: DAW session persistence test

---

## CCC-06: User Creative Control

**Definition:** AI implements DSP; human makes ALL creative decisions (sound identity, aesthetic direction, signal flow, genre focus).

**Applies to phases:** 0 (Specification), 2 (KB Architecture), 4 (DSP Implementation), 7 (UI)

**Human decisions (never AI-assumed):**
- Sound identity words (warm, bright, dark, etc.)
- Genre/target audience
- Visual aesthetic (skeuomorphic, flat, futuristic)
- Pricing level
- Feature scope

**AI decisions (implementation details):**
- DSP algorithms for specified sound
- Code structure
- Test coverage
- Build configuration

**Enforcement:**
- Phase 0: Creative decisions documented in specification
- Phase 4: Reference specification for all creative choices
- Phase 7: Human approval on UI design

---

## CCC-07: Commercial Viability

**Definition:** Plugin is designed for market, not just functionality. Pricing, positioning, and distribution are planned from Phase 0.

**Applies to phases:** 0 (Specification), 10 (Licensing), 11 (Marketplace), 12 (Marketing)

**Components:**
- Value proposition differentiation
- Pricing strategy (tiered vs perpetual)
- Target audience definition
- Marketing channels (achievable by solo developer)

**Enforcement:**
- Phase 0: Market positioning in specification
- Phase 10: Licensing integration complete
- Phase 11: Marketplace listing prepared
- Phase 12: Marketing strategy documented

---

## CCC-08: Knowledge Base Integration

**Definition:** All phases reference and populate the Knowledge Base. The KB bridges sound design vocabulary to DSP parameters.

**Applies to phases:** 2 (KB Architecture), 3 (KB Bootstrapping), all subsequent phases

**KB Layers:**
1. Technical (C++, JUCE, DSP)
2. Sound Design (synthesis, techniques)
3. UI/UX (control design, accessibility)
4. Commercial (licensing, marketing)
5. Reference (academic, textbook citations)

**Enforcement:**
- Phase 2: KB architecture defined
- Phase 3: KB seeded with initial content
- Every phase: Update KB with new learnings

---

## CCC-09: Session Boundary Management

**Definition:** Multi-session workflow is explicit. Each phase defines context that must be preserved across sessions.

**Applies to phases:** All phases

**Session requirements:**
- Decisions ledger updated at every gate
- Artifact manifest current
- All files saved before session end
- Next session can resume from gate state

**Enforcement:**
- Every phase gate: Update tracking files
- Session break: Verify all files saved
- Resume: Load context from tracking files

---

## Cross-Cutting Concerns Summary

| ID | Concern | Phases | Primary Verification |
|----|---------|--------|---------------------|
| CCC-01 | Audio Thread Safety | 4, 7, 8, 9 | Code audit + stress test |
| CCC-02 | Gain Staging | 0, 4, 9 | Metering + extreme input test |
| CCC-03 | Parameter Smoothing | 4, 8 | SmoothedValue + click test |
| CCC-04 | DAW Compatibility | 9, 14 | Multi-DAW testing checklist |
| CCC-05 | State Serialization | 4, 5, 8, 9 | Round-trip tests |
| CCC-06 | User Creative Control | 0, 2, 4, 7 | Human approval gates |
| CCC-07 | Commercial Viability | 0, 10, 11, 12 | Market positioning doc |
| CCC-08 | KB Integration | 2, 3, all | KB updates at gates |
| CCC-09 | Session Boundaries | All | Tracking file currency |

---

*Created: Phase 1 — Domain Research*"
}

{
  "file_path": "/home/myuser/playbooks/vst-product-lifecycle-playbook/research/platform-concerns.md",
  "content": "# Platform & Environment Concerns — Linux VST Development

## Target Platform: Linux Mint + REAPER

This playbook targets Linux Mint as the development platform with REAPER as the primary DAW. This section documents platform-specific requirements, constraints, and best practices.

---

## Linux Development Environment

### Required System Dependencies

```bash
# Essential for JUCE GUI
sudo apt install libx11-xcb-dev libxcb-util-dev libxcb-cursor-dev \
                 libxcb-xkb-dev libxkbcommon-dev libxkbcommon-x11-dev \
                 libfontconfig1-dev libcairo2-dev

# GTK integration (for native file dialogs)
sudo apt install libgtkmm-3.0-dev

# Audio system
sudo apt install libasound2-dev libpulse-dev

# SQLite (if using preset databases)
sudo apt install libsqlite3-dev

# XCB keysyms (for keyboard input)
sudo apt install libxcb-keysyms1-dev
```

### Build Tools

```bash
# CMake (3.22+)
sudo apt install cmake

# Compiler (GCC 7+ or Clang 6+)
sudo apt install build-essential

# Or for Clang
sudo apt install clang
```

---

## JUCE-Specific Configuration

### FetchContent Setup

```cmake
include(FetchContent)

# JUCE 8.0.x
FetchContent_Declare(
    JUCE
    GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/juce-framework/JUCE.git
    GIT_TAG origin/master
)

FetchContent_MakeAvailable(JUCE)

# Your plugin target
juce_add_plugin(MyPlugin
    PRODUCT_NAME "MyPlugin"
    PLUGIN_NAME "MyPlugin"
    # ... other settings
)
```

### Linux-Specific CMake Settings

```cmake
# VST3 output location
set(JUCE_VST3_COPY_DIR "~/.vst3")

# Standalone for testing
juce_add_plugin(MyPlugin
    # ...
    PLUGIN_formats VST3 Standalone
    # Linux needs explicit GUI backend
    JUCE_LINUX_CMAKE_VST3_CAN_EXPORT_XML_GUI 1
)
```

---

## REAPER-Specific Configuration

### Plugin Paths

| Format | Path | Notes |
|--------|------|-------|
| VST3 | `~/.vst3/` | Standard location |
| VST2 | `~/.vst/` | Legacy, still works |
| LV2 | `~/.lv2/` | Linux-native format |
| CLAP | `~/.clap/` | Newer format |

### REAPER Configuration

1. **Options → Preferences → Plug-ins**
   - Add custom paths if using non-standard locations
   - Enable "Clear cache and rescan" after plugin updates

2. **Debugging workflow:**
   ```bash
   # Build
   cmake --build build

   # Plugin automatically copied to ~/.vst3 (if configured)
   # Or manually copy:
   cp build/MyPlugin_artefacts/Release/VST3/MyPlugin.vst3 ~/.vst3/

   # Launch REAPER
   reaper

   # In REAPER: Options → Preferences → Plug-ins → Re-scan
   ```

3. **Plugin Host for debugging:**
   ```bash
   # JUCE provides AudioPluginHost for direct debugging
   # Located in JUCE/extras/AudioPluginHost/
   cmake -B build_host -DJUCE_BUILD_AUDIO_PLUGIN_HOST=ON
   cmake --build build_host
   ./build_host/AudioPluginHost
   ```

---

## Platform-Specific Anti-Patterns

### What NEVER to Do on Linux

| Anti-Pattern | Why It Fails | Correct Approach |
|--------------|--------------|------------------|
| **Assume /usr/bin/** | User may install REAPER elsewhere | Use `which reaper` or `$PATH` |
| **Hardcode .vst3 location** | May differ by distro | Use JUCE's standard copy or `~/.vst3` |
| **Ignore JACK** | Some users run JACK, not PulseAudio | Support both audio systems |
| **Skip ALSA** | PulseAudio sits on ALSA | ALSA is the low-level requirement |
| **Assume GUI thread** | Linux threading differs | Use JUCE's MessageThread |
| **Use Windows paths** | Wine is separate | Native builds, not Wine paths |

### Wine/Yabridge (Not Recommended)

For this playbook:
- **Target:** Native Linux VST3
- **Not covering:** Windows VSTs via Wine/Yabridge
- **Reasoning:** Native builds have fewer compatibility issues

If Windows plugin support is needed in future:
```bash
# Yabridge setup (for Windows plugins)
sudo apt install wine yabridge

# Windows VST paths in Wine
# C:\Program Files\Steinberg\VstPlugins (VST2)
# C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST3 (VST3)
```

---

## Audio System Considerations

### ALSA vs PulseAudio vs JACK

| System | Use Case | Notes |
|--------|----------|-------|
| **ALSA** | Low-level, always available | Required dependency |
| **PulseAudio** | Desktop audio, common on Mint | User-friendly but higher latency |
| **JACK** | Pro audio, low latency | Requires configuration, not default |

**Plugin behavior:** Plugins don't choose — DAW handles audio system. Plugin just processes buffers.

### Latency Considerations

- **Buffer size matters:** Test at 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024 samples
- **Sample rate matters:** Test at 44100, 48000, 96000 Hz
- **REAPER reporting:** Plugin must report latency accurately if introduced

---

## Testing on Linux

### Primary DAW: REAPER

```bash
# Install REAPER (if not installed)
# Download from https://www.reaper.fm/download.php
# Linux version is .tar.xz archive

tar -xf reaper*.tar.xz
cd reaper_linux_*
./install-reaper.sh

# Launch
reaper
```

### Secondary DAWs for Compatibility Testing

| DAW | Availability | Notes |
|-----|--------------|-------|
| **Bitwig Studio** | Commercial, Linux native | Modern DAW, good compatibility |
| **Ardour** | Open source | Different threading model |
| **Tracktion Waveform Free** | Free, Linux native | Different UI framework |

### Plugin Validation Tools

```bash
# JUCE's pluginval (cross-platform)
# Download from: https://github.com/Tracktion/pluginval

pluginval --validate-in-process ~/.vst3/MyPlugin.vst3

# Tests:
# - State serialization
# - Parameter thread safety
# - Audio processing edge cases
# - Multiple sample rates/buffer sizes
```

---

## Distribution for Linux

### VST3 Bundle Structure

```
MyPlugin.vst3/
├── Contents/
│   ├── Info.plist (not used on Linux, but present for compatibility)
│   └── x86_64-linux/
│       └── MyPlugin.so
```

### Installation

```bash
# User installation
cp -r MyPlugin.vst3 ~/.vst3/

# System installation (requires sudo)
sudo cp -r MyPlugin.vst3 /usr/lib/vst3/
```

### Archive for Distribution

```bash
# Create distributable archive
tar -czvf MyPlugin-Linux.tar.gz MyPlugin.vst3

# User extracts and installs
tar -xzvf MyPlugin-Linux.tar.gz
cp -r MyPlugin.vst3 ~/.vst3/
```

---

## Cross-Platform Considerations (Future)

This playbook targets Linux first. Future versions should address:

| Platform | Key Differences | Effort Level |
|----------|-----------------|--------------|
| **macOS** | Code signing, notarization, AU format | Medium |
| **Windows** | VST3 path differs, no code signing required | Low |

### macOS Quick Reference (Future)

```bash
# Build for Mac
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES="arm64;x86_64"
cmake --build build

# VST3 location
~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3/

# AU location
~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/Components/

# Code signing required
codesign --force --deep --sign "Developer ID" MyPlugin.vst3
```

### Windows Quick Reference (Future)

```powershell
# VST3 location
C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST3\

# Build with Visual Studio
cmake -B build -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64
cmake --build build --config Release
```

---

## Platform Concerns Summary

| Concern | Linux-Specific | General |
|---------|----------------|---------|
| Build system | CMake + FetchContent | Same |
| Dependencies | libx11-*, libgtkmm | Different per platform |
| VST3 location | ~/.vst3 | Platform-specific |
| Testing DAW | REAPER | Multiple DAWs recommended |
| Code signing | Not required | Mac requires |
| Audio system | ALSA/PulseAudio | Plugin-agnostic |

---

*Created: Phase 1 — Domain Research*"
}
